nameStory: The name 'spinifera' comes from Latin meaning 'spine-bearing,' referring to the distinctive spiny projections found on this tiny spider's body. As the only member of its genus Souessa, it's like finding a rare single gem in nature's jewelry box.
description: Souessa spinifera is an extremely rare sheet weaver spider that belongs to the family of tiny web-building spiders. This minuscule arachnid creates delicate sheet webs to catch prey, like most of its relatives in the Linyphiidae family. It's one of New England's most elusive spiders, with only a handful of confirmed sightings in the region. Being a sheet weaver, it's quite small - likely less than a few millimeters in body length.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Look for delicate, horizontal sheet webs stretched between vegetation or in sheltered spots, feeling almost silky-smooth when accidentally brushed

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely tiny spider with characteristic spiny projections on the abdomen that feel rigid if gently touched with a fine brush

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Minuscule even by sheet weaver standards - smaller than most ants you'd encounter, requiring close examination or magnification to observe details

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Stays close to or underneath its sheet web, often hanging upside down and running quickly across the silk when disturbed

idTips.label: Habitat Clues
idTips.description: Found in very specific microhabitats that remain somewhat mysterious due to its rarity - likely among leaf litter or low vegetation

habitat: The exact habitat preferences of Souessa spinifera remain largely mysterious due to its extreme rarity in New England. Based on the few confirmed sightings, it likely inhabits sheltered microenvironments such as dense leaf litter, low-growing vegetation, or protected spaces near the ground. It probably prefers areas with stable moisture and protection from direct sunlight.

seasonality.spring: Peak activity period may occur in late spring when many sheet weavers become active, though specific timing is poorly documented for this rare species.
seasonality.summer: Likely active during summer months when most sheet weaver spiders are hunting and web-building, but observations are too rare to establish clear patterns.
seasonality.fall: May be found in early fall, possibly when mating occurs, though the reproductive timing of this species remains largely unknown.
seasonality.winter: Probably overwinters in protected locations like deep leaf litter or under logs, remaining inactive during cold months.

funFact: Souessa spinifera is so rare that it's been found only twice in all of New England, making it potentially rarer than finding a four-leaf clover - which statistically occurs once in every 5,000 clovers!
confusionNotes: Due to its extreme rarity and tiny size, this spider is most likely to be overlooked entirely rather than confused with other species. Other small sheet weavers in the region lack the characteristic spiny projections that give this species its name.
contextualKnowledge: This spider represents a monotypic genus, meaning Souessa spinifera is the only species in its entire genus worldwide. Finding one would be like discovering a living fossil - a unique evolutionary branch with no close relatives.
compareHints: Since Souessa spinifera is the only species in its genus, it's truly one-of-a-kind among New England spiders. Compared to other sheet weavers in the Linyphiidae family, it's distinguished by its spiny body projections and extreme rarity. Most other small sheet weavers you'll encounter will be from much more common genera like Lepthyphantes or Linyphia, which lack the distinctive spines and are far more frequently observed.
